title: Abdominal Pain
hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} is a 22-year-old woman with no known past medical history who presents to the emergency department with diffuse abdominal pain, lethargy, and vomiting for two days. She reports increased appetite prior to symptom onset, along with blurry vision, dizziness, drowsiness, and polyuria. She is on oral contraceptives and has a family history of diabetes in a sibling. Exam reveals dry mucous membranes, decreased skin turgor, and tachycardia. Point-of-care glucose is markedly elevated in the 600s. The clinical picture is consistent with new-onset diabetic ketoacidosis — the abdominal pain is a common presenting feature of DKA, not a primary surgical abdomen.
chief_complaint: Abdominal pain, vomiting, lethargy x 2 days

stacks.label: Physical Exam: General Appearance
stacks.finding: The general examination is extremely useful to determine how sick the patient looks.

stacks.label: Physical Exam: Chest / Lungs
stacks.finding: Patient in moderate distress — important to look for pulmonary problems.

stacks.label: Physical Exam: Heart / Cardiovascular
stacks.finding: Patient in moderate distress — important to look for cardiovascular problems.

stacks.label: Physical Exam: Abdomen
stacks.finding: This is the presenting chief complaint — abdominal exam is required.

stacks.label: Physical Exam: Genitalia
stacks.finding: Pelvic pain can present as abdominal pain — should be examined.

stacks.label: Physical Exam: HEENT / Neck
stacks.finding: Will show dry mucous membranes — key finding in DKA.

stacks.label: Physical Exam: Skin
stacks.finding: Will show low skin turgor from dehydration.

stacks.label: HCG, beta, urine/serum qualitative
stacks.finding: Every female patient of childbearing age should have a pregnancy test done.

stacks.label: Hemoglobin A1C, blood
stacks.finding: Expected to be elevated with new-onset diabetes. Not required for acute management.

stacks.label: Arterial blood gases
stacks.finding: ABGs are not required in DKA. Bicarbonate levels and anion gap are sufficient to monitor correction. Best way to monitor DKA resolution is disappearance of elevated anion gap.

stacks.label: Urinalysis
stacks.finding: Important to see extent of chronic diabetes. Patient spilling protein into urine with normal creatinine.

stacks.label: CBC with differential
stacks.finding: Important to rule out infection. Leukocyte count is high — DKA patients often have elevated counts from catecholamine release and dehydration.

stacks.label: Basic metabolic profile / Comprehensive metabolic profile
stacks.finding: Will find extremely high blood glucose. Important to monitor electrolytes — DKA can cause pseudohypercalcemia.

stacks.label: Insulin (regular / lispro / glargine / NPH)
stacks.finding: Mainstay treatment for DKA is insulin. Patient will slowly improve once insulin treatment initiated.

stacks.label: Normal saline / Lactated Ringer / 0.45% saline
stacks.finding: IV fluids should be given to every DKA patient. Normal saline or LR if sodium is normal.

stacks.label: Potassium replacement (KCl / K citrate / K phosphate)
stacks.finding: Potassium must be checked prior to insulin therapy — insulin worsens pre-existing hypokalemia, risking fatal cardiac arrhythmias. Start replacement if K < 5.3. KCl is preferred as patients are chloride-depleted.

stacks.label: Intravenous access
stacks.finding: Good practice to order IV access when administering IV fluids/medications.

stacks.label: Dextrose solutions
stacks.finding: Patient is already hyperglycemic in the 600s — additional glucose is not warranted. Glucose can be added once levels reach 250 range, but should not be used during initial treatment.

stacks.label: Papanicolaou smear / HPV DNA test
stacks.finding: Patient has not had a recent pap smear — this should be done.

stacks.label: Tdap vaccine
stacks.finding: Tdap should be given every 10 years. No history given — should be administered.

stacks.label: HPV vaccine
stacks.finding: HPV vaccine should be given to females ages 11-26.

stacks.label: Advise patient, no illegal drug use
stacks.finding: If patient admits to illicit drug use, it is important to advise against use.

stacks.label: Instruct patient, diabetes
stacks.finding: Patient needs diabetes education about proper glucose management after discharge.

physical_exam.cardiovascular: Tachycardic — HR elevated from dehydration and acidosis.
physical_exam.respiratory: Assess for Kussmaul respirations (deep, rapid breathing compensating for metabolic acidosis).
physical_exam.abdominal: Diffuse abdominal tenderness. Abdominal pain is a common presenting symptom of DKA — may mimic acute abdomen.
physical_exam.neurological: Alert but drowsy; assess for cerebral edema if mental status deteriorates.
physical_exam.skin: Decreased skin turgor from dehydration. Dry.
physical_exam.heent: Dry mucous membranes — classic DKA finding.

decoys.label: CT abdomen/pelvis with contrast
decoys.reason_wrong: While abdominal pain warrants investigation, markedly elevated glucose (600s) with anion gap acidosis is diagnostic of DKA. Treat the DKA first — the pain resolves with insulin and fluids.

decoys.label: Broad-spectrum antibiotics
decoys.reason_wrong: Leukocytosis in DKA is caused by catecholamine release and dehydration, not infection. No evidence of infectious source.

decoys.label: Surgical consult for acute abdomen
decoys.reason_wrong: Abdominal pain in DKA can mimic acute abdomen but resolves with metabolic correction. Surgery is not indicated.

decoys.label: Dextrose-containing fluids initially
decoys.reason_wrong: Patient has glucose in the 600s. Dextrose would worsen hyperglycemia. Only add dextrose once glucose reaches ~250 mg/dL.

teach_me_steps.order: Diagnose DKA: glucose + anion gap + ketones
teach_me_steps.reasoning: DKA triad: hyperglycemia, metabolic acidosis with elevated anion gap, and ketonemia/ketonuria. Abdominal pain is a common presenting feature.
Fluid resuscitation is the first step. DKA patients are profoundly dehydrated. Normal saline or LR if Na is normal.
Regular insulin IV drip (or SQ lispro). Corrects hyperglycemia and halts ketogenesis.
Check K before insulin. Insulin drives K intracellularly — can cause fatal hypokalemia. Start replacement if K < 5.3.
Best marker for DKA resolution is disappearance of elevated anion gap, not normalization of glucose.
DKA requires ICU monitoring. Insulin drip, frequent labs (q2h glucose and electrolytes), and close observation.

case_summary: New-onset Type 1 Diabetes presenting as DKA. Glucose in 600s. Treatment: IV fluids + insulin + K replacement. Monitor anion gap for resolution. Admit to ICU. Preventive: diabetes education, pap smear, HPV/Tdap vaccines, drug counseling.
